title: Python Data Structures and OOP
summary: Data structures are how you organize information in memory. Choosing the right one (list vs dict vs set) affects performance and clarity. Object-oriented programming lets you model real-world things as objects with data (attributes) and behavior (met
content:
# Python Data Structures and OOP ##### The chatbot that got slower every day A student in Coimbatore built a customer-support retrieval bot for her college project. It searched a list of 12,000 FAQ entries and returned the closest match. On day one it answered in 40 milliseconds. By the time she demoed it with the full dataset loaded, each answer took nearly four seconds — and the demo had a live audience. The culprit was one line: ```python if question_id in seen_ids: # seen_ids was a list ``` Checking membership in a **list** means Python walks it from the start, comparing one element at a time. With 12,000 entries and a check inside a loop over 12,000 questions, that is 144 million comparisons. She changed `seen_ids = []` to `seen_ids = set()`. Nothing else. Answers came back in 60 milliseconds. That is the difference a data structure makes, and it is not a micro-optimisation — it is a factor of sixty. Today is about knowing which container to reach for, and then about **objects**, which are how you stop your GenAI code from becoming a tangle of loose functions and dictionaries nobody can follow. ##### The four core containers | Type | Written as | Ordered? | Changeable? | Duplicates? | Membership check | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | **list** | `[1, 2, 3]` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Slow — O(n) | | **tuple** | `(1, 2, 3)` | Yes | **No** | Yes | Slow — O(n) | | **set** | `{1, 2, 3}` | No | Yes | **No** | **Fast — O(1)** | | **dict** | `{"a": 1}` | Yes (insertion) | Yes | Keys unique | **Fast — O(1)** | That last column is the Coimbatore lesson. Sets and dicts use **hashing**: Python computes a number from the value and jumps straight to where it would be stored. Lists have to look. **Lists** — ordered, changeable sequences. Your default for "several of the same kind of thing." ```python chunks = ["intro paragraph", "policy section", "appendix"] chunks.append("summary") # add to end chunks.insert(0, "title") # add at position chunks.extend(["notes", "refs"]) # add several last = chunks.pop() # remove and return last chunks.remove("appendix") # remove by value print(chunks[0]) # 'title' print(chunks[-1]) # last item print(chunks[1:3]) # slice — items 1 and 2 print(len(chunks)) ``` **Tuples** — like lists but immutable. Use them for things that should not change: coordinates, RGB colours, a fixed pair of values, or a dictionary key. ```python embedding_dims = (1536,) # note the comma for a 1-tuple model_config = ("gpt-4o-mini", 0.7, 512) name, temp, tokens = model_config # unpacking ``` Immutability is a feature. If a value should never change, a tuple makes accidental change impossible. **Sets** — unordered collections of unique items. Reach for these for deduplication and fast membership. ```python tags_a = {"rag", "embeddings", "python"} tags_b = {"python", "agents", "rag"} print(tags_a | tags_b) # union → everything print(tags_a & tags_b) # intersection → {'rag', 'python'} print(tags_a - tags_b) # difference → {'embeddings'} seen = set() for doc_id in incoming_ids: if doc_id in seen: # O(1) — instant, regardless of size continue seen.add(doc_id) process(doc_id) ``` **Dicts** — key→value lookups. The single most important structure in GenAI work, because JSON is a dict. ```python response = { "id": "chatcmpl-abc123", "model": "gpt-4o-mini", "usage": {"prompt_tokens": 412, "completion_tokens": 88}, "choices": [ {"index": 0, "message": {"role": "assistant", "content": "Here is..."}} ], } text = response["choices"][0]["message"]["content"] # .get() returns None (or a default) instead of crashing on a missing key finish = response.get("finish_reason", "unknown") for key, value in response["usage"].items(): print(f"{key}: {value}") ``` `.get()` versus `[]` is a real decision. Use `[]` when the key must exist (and you want a loud failure if it does not). Use `.get()` when it is genuinely optional. ##### Comprehensions A comprehension builds a new collection from an existing one in a single expression. Once it clicks, you will read Python much faster. ```python chunks = [" Intro ", "", "Policy details", " ", "Appendix A"] # Long form cleaned = [] for c in chunks: if c.strip(): cleaned.append(c.strip().lower()) # Comprehension — same thing cleaned = [c.strip().lower() for c in chunks if c.strip()] ``` The shape is always: `[EXPRESSION for ITEM in ITERABLE if CONDITION]`. They work for the other containers too: ```python lengths = {c: len(c) for c in cleaned} # dict comprehension unique_ws = {w for c in cleaned for w in c.split()} # set comprehension ``` **When not to use one:** if it needs more than one condition and a nested loop, or if it will not fit comfortably on one line, write the explicit loop. Comprehensions are for clarity, and a comprehension nobody can read has failed at its only job. ##### Classes and objects A **class** is a blueprint. An **object** (or instance) is a thing built from that blueprint. The point is bundling data with the behaviour that operates on it. Without classes, a document store looks like loose dicts and functions floating around your file, and nothing stops someone passing the wrong dict to the wrong function. With a class: ```python from datetime import datetime, timezone class Document: """A single document in a knowledge base.""" def __init__(self, doc_id: str, title: str, text: str, tags=None): self.doc_id = doc_id self.title = title self.text = text self.tags = set(tags) if tags else set() self.created_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc) def word_count(self) -> int: return len(self.text.split()) def chunk(self, size: int = 200) -> list[str]: """Split into word-based chunks for embedding.""" words = self.text.split() return [" ".join(words[i:i + size]) for i in range(0, len(words), size)] def add_tag(self, tag: str) -> None: self.tags.add(tag.lower().strip()) def __repr__(self) -> str: return f"Document(id={self.doc_id!r}, title={self.title!r}, words={self.word_count()})" doc = Document("d-001", "Leave Policy", "Employees may take " * 300, tags=["hr"]) doc.add_tag("Policy") print(doc) # Document(id='d-001', title='Leave Policy', words=900) print(len(doc.chunk(200))) # 5 ``` The vocabulary: - **`__init__`** — the constructor. Runs automatically when you create an object; sets up its initial state. - **`self`** — the instance itself. Every method takes it as the first parameter, and it is how a method reaches the object's own data. You never pass it explicitly; Python does. - **Attribute** — data on the object (`doc.title`). - **Method** — a function belonging to the object (`doc.chunk()`). - **`__repr__`** — what Python prints. Define it; debugging without it is miserable. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["class Document
(the blueprint)"] --> B["doc1 = Document('d-001', ...)"] A --> C["doc2 = Document('d-002', ...)"] A --> D["doc3 = Document('d-003', ...)"] B --> E["own data:
title, text, tags"] C --> F["own data:
title, text, tags"] D --> G["own data:
title, text, tags"] A --> H["shared behaviour:
word_count(), chunk(), add_tag()"] ``` ##### Inheritance Inheritance lets a class build on another. The child gets everything the parent has, and can add or override. ```python class PDFDocument(Document): """A Document that came from a PDF and knows its page count.""" def __init__(self, doc_id, title, text, page_count, tags=None): super().__init__(doc_id, title, text, tags) # run the parent's setup self.page_count = page_count self.add_tag("pdf") def chunk(self, size: int = 200) -> list[str]: """Override: PDFs get smaller chunks because layout adds noise.""" return super().chunk(size=min(size, 120)) def __repr__(self) -> str: return f"PDFDocument(id={self.doc_id!r}, pages={self.page_count})" pdf = PDFDocument("d-009", "Compliance Manual", "text " * 5000, page_count=412) print(pdf.word_count()) # inherited, unchanged print(len(pdf.chunk())) # overridden behaviour print(isinstance(pdf, Document)) # True ``` `super()` calls the parent's version. Use it in `__init__` so the parent's setup still runs. **A caution:** beginners over-use inheritance. The honest rule is that inheritance expresses "is-a" — a `PDFDocument` *is a* `Document`. If the relationship is "has-a" (a `ContactBook` *has* `Contact`s), use composition: just store them as an attribute. The *Design Patterns* book's advice to "favour composition over inheritance" is forty years old and still right. ##### Exception handling Things fail. Files are missing, APIs time out, users type letters where you expected numbers. Exceptions let you handle failure without the whole program dying. ```python import json def load_config(path: str) -> dict: try: with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f: config = json.load(f) except FileNotFoundError: print(f"No config at {path}; using defaults.") return {"model": "gpt-4o-mini", "temperature": 0.7} except json.JSONDecodeError as exc: raise ValueError(f"Config at {path} is not valid JSON: {exc}") from exc else: print("Config loaded.") return config finally: print("load_config finished.") ``` The four blocks: `try` holds the risky code; `except` handles a specific failure; `else` runs only if nothing was raised; `finally` runs always, which is where cleanup goes. **Raise your own** when a caller has done something invalid: ```python class MissingFieldError(Exception): """A record is missing a required field.""" def validate(record: dict) -> None: for field in ("id", "text"): if field not in record: raise MissingFieldError(f"Record is missing required field: {field!r}") ``` Custom exception classes cost two lines and let callers catch exactly your error rather than everything. **The cardinal sin:** ```python try: risky() except: # catches EVERYTHING, including Ctrl-C and typos pass # and then silently hides it ``` This turns a crash you could have fixed in five minutes into a mystery you will chase for two days. Catch specific exceptions. If you must catch broadly, use `except Exception as exc:` and at minimum log it. ##### Modules and packages A **module** is one `.py` file. A **package** is a folder of modules. ``` contactbook/ ├── __init__.py # marks the folder as a package ├── models.py # Contact, ContactBook classes ├── storage.py # save_json, load_json └── cli.py # the command-line interface main.py ``` ```python # main.py from contactbook.models import Contact, ContactBook from contactbook.storage import save_json book = ContactBook() book.add(Contact("Anjali Rao", "anjali@example.com", "+91-98200-11223")) save_json(book, "contacts.json") ``` Splitting code into modules is not ceremony. It is what makes a 600-line project navigable, testable, and reusable — and it is exactly how every library you import is built. ##### Common mistakes - **Using a list where a set belongs** for membership checks — the four-second demo. - **Mutating a list while looping over it.** Iterate over a copy (`for x in items[:]`) or build a new list. - **Forgetting `self`** in a method signature, then getting a confusing argument-count error. - **Shared mutable class attributes.** `class C: items = []` gives *every* instance the same list. Initialise mutable state in `__init__`. - **Bare `except:` with `pass`** — silently swallowing bugs. - **Inheriting when composing would be clearer.** - **Over-clever comprehensions** with three nested loops. - **`dict[key]` on data you did not create**, crashing on the one API response that omitted a field. Use `.get()`. - **No `__repr__`**, so printing an object gives `<__main__.Document object at 0x7f...>`. - **Circular imports** — module A imports B which imports A. Usually a sign your responsibilities are split wrongly. ##### Hands-on: model something real Your practical task is a `Dataset` class holding a list of records, with methods to add, filter, and summarise — and error handling for records missing a field. Make `add()` validate and raise your own `MissingFieldError`. Make `filter()` take a function as an argument so callers can pass any condition. And write a `__repr__` that prints the record count. That is a genuinely reusable class, not an exercise. The mini project — a contact book with `Contact` and `ContactBook` classes plus JSON persistence — is the composition pattern in miniature. `ContactBook` *has* contacts; it should not inherit from anything. Store them in a dict keyed by name or ID so lookup is instant, not in a list you have to scan. Saving to JSON will teach you the small, useful lesson that a `set` is not JSON-serialisable and needs converting to a list first. The assignment refactors Day 1's budget calculator into a `Budget` class with exception handling. This is a real skill — turning working procedural code into an object without changing what it does. Keep the old script; run both and confirm identical output. That habit, verifying a refactor preserves behaviour, is what separates confident engineers from hopeful ones. ##### Key takeaways - **Choose the container by the operation you do most**: lists for ordered sequences, tuples for fixed values, **sets for fast membership and deduplication**, dicts for key lookup and every piece of JSON you touch. - **Comprehensions build collections in one readable line** — but drop back to an explicit loop the moment readability suffers. - **Classes bundle data with the behaviour that acts on it**; `__init__` sets up state, `self` reaches it, and `__repr__` saves you during debugging. - **Prefer composition to inheritance.** Use inheritance only for genuine "is-a" relationships, and call `super().__init__()` when you do. - **Catch specific exceptions, never bare `except: pass`**, and split growing code into modules and packages before it becomes unnavigable.
practical_task_reference: Create a 'Dataset' class that stores a list of records, with methods to add, filter, and summarize records. Handle errors when a record is missing a field.
mini_project_reference: Build a mini contact book with a Contact class and a ContactBook class supporting add, search, delete, and save to a JSON file.
